To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
highly institutionalized multilateral organizations acting as institutional entrepreneurship need to manage two tensions: legitimacy management and change management.

highly institutionalized organizational actors acting as institutional entrepreneurs have to simultaneously manage the tensions between legitimacy management (e.g., managing the legitimacy of the change process) and change process management (e.g. managing the legitimacy of change) in order to influence institutional change.

institutional entrepreneurs need to be able to: (a) identify and manage the tensions of legitimacy management and change management, (b) manage the tensions of the change process, (c) manage the tensions between the internal and external environments, and (d) manage the tensions in their own organizations.

understanding the dynamic capabilities of institutional entrepreneurs.

we have found that the institutional entrepreneurs in the UNDP case had the capabilities to create change, but they did not have the capabilities to manage that change.
the capabilities required to succeed in institutional entrepreneurship are dynamic and are shaped by the context of the institutional entrepreneur.
the capabilities needed to change an institution are the same capabilities needed to change the organization.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the capabilities required to succeed as an institutional entrepreneur are not just about managing change processes, but also managing the legitimacy challenges that are created by those processes.
organizations acting as institutional entrepreneur need to manage the tension between managing their legitimacy in the field and managing the process of change in order to succeed.
organizations need to be able to manage two key dynamic capabilities – legitimacy management and process management – to successfully change their institutional fields.
